word_order: SVO | subjects precede verbs and verbs precede objects in examples such as 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device' and 'The capsule will look much like a shooting star'.
register: edited written informational prose (news reports, encyclopedic and technical descriptive text)
discourse_markers: temporal prepositional linkers (after the war, prior to)
clause_boundary_signals: relative pronouns introducing embedded clauses (who, which)
non_boundary_traps: initial temporal/prepositional adjuncts that look like sentence-openers but attach to a following clause (for over a thousand years, around 60)
verbal adjuncts/gerundial phrases introduced by by/to that are subordinate (by walking, to have)
embedded relative or participial modifiers inside NPs that contain clause-like structure (those who are employed, the atoms emitting photons)
parenthetical adverbials that look clause-final or -initial but do not end the clause (in the end, of course)
unstable_prefix_signals: sentence-initial focusing/limiting item whose scope can be revised by continuation (only)
initial subordinating/adverbial linkers whose function and scope are resolved only after the main clause appears (although, because)
approximate quantifiers that may narrow or shift scope as continuation arrives (around)
notes_for_prompt_writer: The samples are formal written English with canonical SVO order and frequent embedded clauses introduced by complementizers and relative pronouns. Many modifiers (prepositional phrases, by-/to- verbal phrases, relative clauses) are clause-internal and should not be taken as sentence boundaries. Sentence-initial focused items (e.g. only) and subordinating adverbials leave scope and attachment ambiguous until the remainder of the sentence is seen.
